name: Pastel de Nata
description: A crisp puff-pastry tart filled with egg custard, often dusted with cinnamon. Originally sold as Pastéis de Belém near the Jerónimos Monastery, it is Portugal's best-known pastry.
how_to_eat: Eat warm, sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar, with a bica.
how_to_order: Ask for 'um pastel de nata' at any pastelaria, or 'pastéis de Belém' in Belém.

name: Bacalhau à Brás
description: Shredded salt cod with onions and matchstick fried potatoes, bound with scrambled eggs and topped with olives and parsley. It is one of the most popular of Portugal's many salt-cod dishes.
how_to_eat: Eat hot, with black olives on top.
how_to_order: Order 'bacalhau à Brás' in Lisbon tascas.

name: Ginjinha
description: A liqueur made by infusing sour Morello cherries (ginja) in aguardente with sugar. Lisbon has historic ginjinha bars such as Ginjinha Espinheira (since 1840).
how_to_eat: Drink a small shot, 'com elas' (with the cherries) or 'sem elas' (without).
how_to_order: Order 'uma ginja' at a ginjinha bar near Rossio.

name: Bifana
description: A bread roll filled with thin pork slices marinated in garlic and white wine. It is eaten all over Portugal and may have first been made in Vendas Novas.
how_to_eat: Eat by hand, with mustard and a cold beer.
how_to_order: Order 'uma bifana' at a snack bar or café counter.

name: Travesseiro de Sintra
description: A rectangular puff-pastry 'pillow' filled with almond and egg cream and dusted with sugar. It was created in the 1940s at the Piriquita bakery in Sintra.
how_to_eat: Eat fresh and warm.
how_to_order: Buy at Sintra's historic pastry shops.

name: Queijada de Sintra
description: A small tart filled with fresh cow's cheese, sugar, egg yolks, flour and cinnamon. It is older than the travesseiro and is Sintra's traditional sweet.
how_to_eat: Eat as a snack with coffee.
how_to_order: Buy at Sintra pastry shops such as Piriquita.

name: Francesinha
description: A layered sandwich of toasted bread, steak, ham and sausages, covered in melted cheese and a hot tomato-and-beer sauce. It originated in Porto.
how_to_eat: Eat with a knife and fork, with fries to dip in the sauce.
how_to_order: Order 'uma francesinha' at Porto cafés, optionally 'com ovo' (with egg).

name: Tripas à Moda do Porto
description: A stew of beef tripe with white beans, carrots, sausage and other meats, served with rice. It is Porto's traditional dish and gives locals their nickname 'tripeiros'.
how_to_eat: Eat with white rice.
how_to_order: Order 'tripas à moda do Porto' in traditional Porto restaurants.

name: Caldo Verde
description: A soup of finely shredded Portuguese cabbage (couve-galega) in a potato and olive oil broth, usually with a slice of chouriço. It comes from the Minho and is eaten all over Portugal.
how_to_eat: Eat hot with broa corn bread.
how_to_order: Order 'caldo verde' as a starter, also sold at festivals.

name: Port Wine
description: A sweet fortified wine made in the Douro Valley and aged in Vila Nova de Gaia. 'Porto' is a protected designation of origin.
how_to_eat: Drink as a dessert wine or aperitif.
how_to_order: Taste it in the port lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia.

name: Vinho Verde
description: A young, often slightly sparkling wine from the protected Vinho Verde region of the Minho. Alvarinho is its best-known white grape.
how_to_eat: Drink chilled with seafood.
how_to_order: Order a bottle of 'vinho verde' in any northern restaurant.

name: Alheira
description: A smoked sausage of bread and meats such as poultry or game, flavoured with garlic. It is from Trás-os-Montes; the Vinhais and Barroso-Montalegre varieties are EU PGI.
how_to_eat: Eat fried with chips and a fried egg.
how_to_order: Order 'alheira com batata frita e ovo' in northern tascas.

name: Polvo à Lagareiro
description: Roasted octopus drenched in olive oil and garlic with punched potatoes (batatas a murro) and turnip greens. It is common in Trás-os-Montes and often eaten on Christmas Eve.
how_to_eat: Eat with the potatoes soaked in the garlic oil.
how_to_order: Order 'polvo à lagareiro' in seafood or traditional restaurants.

name: Leitão da Bairrada
description: Roast suckling pig with crisp skin, roasted in wood-fired ovens. It is the signature dish of the Bairrada area near Mealhada.
how_to_eat: Eat with orange slices, chips, salad and local sparkling wine.
how_to_order: Order at roadside 'leitão' restaurants around Mealhada.

name: Chanfana
description: Old goat meat marinated in plenty of red wine and slow-roasted in a black clay pot, traditionally in a wood oven. Miranda do Corvo and Vila Nova de Poiares both claim it.
how_to_eat: Eat with boiled potatoes.
how_to_order: Order 'chanfana' in Coimbra-area restaurants.

name: Ovos Moles de Aveiro
description: A sweet cream of egg yolks and sugar inside thin wafer shells shaped like fish and seashells. It has been an EU protected geographical indication since 2008-2009.
how_to_eat: Eat whole, wafer and all.
how_to_order: Buy at Aveiro confectioners, often in painted wooden barrels.

name: Pastel de Tentúgal
description: An ultra-thin, crisp pastry of only water and flour, filled with ovos moles egg cream. Created by Carmelite nuns in Tentúgal in the 16th century, it is an EU PGI.
how_to_eat: Eat fresh, dusted with sugar.
how_to_order: Buy in Tentúgal or Coimbra pastry shops.

name: Pão de Ló de Ovar
description: A moist sponge cake of eggs, sugar and flour, made without yeast or baking powder. The Ovar version, with a soft runny centre, has been an EU PGI since 2016.
how_to_eat: Eat by the slice, especially at Easter.
how_to_order: Buy from bakeries in Ovar.

name: Serra da Estrela Cheese
description: A soft-to-runny sheep's milk cheese from the Serra da Estrela mountains, curdled with thistle. 'Queijo Serra da Estrela' is an EU PDO.
how_to_eat: Cut off the top rind and scoop the soft cheese with bread.
how_to_order: Buy at markets and cheese shops in the Serra da Estrela.

name: Licor Beirão
description: A herbal liqueur from Lousã in the Beira region, made since the 19th century. It is the most consumed spirit in Portugal.
how_to_eat: Drink neat or with ice as a digestif.
how_to_order: Ask for 'um Beirão' at any bar.

name: Carne de Porco à Alentejana
description: Cubes of pork marinated in white wine, paprika and garlic, fried and combined with clams, potatoes and coriander. It is one of Portugal's best-known pork dishes.
how_to_eat: Eat with the fried potato cubes and pickles.
how_to_order: Order it in Alentejo and Lisbon tascas.

name: Açorda Alentejana
description: A bread soup of stale bread with garlic, coriander, olive oil and poached eggs in hot water. It is the Alentejo's classic peasant dish.
how_to_eat: Eat hot, breaking the poached egg into the bread.
how_to_order: Order 'açorda alentejana' in Alentejo restaurants.

name: Migas
description: Fried crumbs of stale bread with garlic and olive oil, a shepherds' dish. In the Alentejo it usually accompanies fried pork.
how_to_eat: Eat as a side with pork.
how_to_order: Order 'migas com carne de porco' in Alentejo taverns.

name: Sericaia
description: A soufflé-like egg pudding baked in a clay dish and sprinkled with cinnamon, from Elvas. It is served with stewed Elvas greengage plums.
how_to_eat: Eat with a syrupy plum on top.
how_to_order: Order 'sericaia com ameixa de Elvas' in Alentejo restaurants.

name: Cataplana
description: A seafood stew of clams, fish or shellfish cooked in a hinged copper pan of the same name. It is the typical dish of the Algarve.
how_to_eat: Share from the pan at the table with bread.
how_to_order: Order 'cataplana de marisco' for two in Algarve restaurants.

name: Grilled Sardines
description: Whole fresh sardines grilled over charcoal with coarse salt. They are Portugal's summer food, cooked at Lisbon's Santo António festivals and in Portimão.
how_to_eat: Eat on a slice of bread or with boiled potatoes and salad.
how_to_order: Order 'sardinhas assadas' in summer at harbour grills.

name: Medronho
description: A strong fruit brandy distilled from the berries of the strawberry tree that grows wild in the Algarve hills. It is the region's traditional spirit.
how_to_eat: Drink a small shot after a meal.
how_to_order: Ask for 'um medronho' in Algarve bars and restaurants.

name: Dom Rodrigo
description: A conventual sweet of egg-yolk threads (fios de ovos) and almonds in sugar syrup, wrapped in colourful foil. It comes from Lagos.
how_to_eat: Unwrap the foil and eat with a spoon.
how_to_order: Buy at Algarve pastry shops.

name: Cozido das Furnas
description: A meat and vegetable stew cooked for hours in pots buried in the volcanic ground of Furnas. It is the most famous dish of São Miguel.
how_to_eat: Eat at lunchtime in Furnas, after the pots come out of the ground.
how_to_order: Book 'cozido das Furnas' ahead at Furnas restaurants.

name: Alcatra
description: Beef marinated in red wine and spices, then slow-cooked in a clay pot. It is the signature dish of Terceira island.
how_to_eat: Eat with bread or sweet massa sovada to soak up the sauce.
how_to_order: Order 'alcatra' in Terceira restaurants.

name: Bolo Lêvedo
description: A slightly sweet, round flat bread from Furnas on São Miguel. It is eaten at any meal and used for sandwiches and burgers.
how_to_eat: Eat toasted with butter or jam.
how_to_order: Buy at bakeries and cafés in the Azores.

name: Lapas
description: Limpets cooked on a griddle in butter, garlic and lemon, sometimes served raw. They are eaten all over the islands.
how_to_eat: Eat straight from the hot pan, dipping bread in the butter.
how_to_order: Order 'lapas grelhadas' at seaside restaurants.

name: São Jorge Cheese
description: A semi-hard, spicy cow's milk cheese from São Jorge island. It is a protected designation of origin (DOP).
how_to_eat: Eat in slices with bread.
how_to_order: Buy at Azorean markets and cheese shops.

name: Espetada
description: Chunks of beef rubbed with garlic, salt and bay leaf, grilled on skewers. It is Madeira's festival meat dish.
how_to_eat: Eat off the skewer hanging at the table, with bolo do caco.
how_to_order: Order 'espetada' in Madeira restaurants.

name: Bolo do Caco
description: A round flatbread from Madeira and Porto Santo, traditionally cooked on a flat basalt slab (caco). It is usually served with garlic butter.
how_to_eat: Eat warm with garlic butter or as a sandwich.
how_to_order: Buy at cafés, markets and street stalls on Madeira.

name: Poncha
description: Madeira's traditional drink of sugar-cane aguardente, honey, sugar and orange or lemon juice. It is the island's best-known drink.
how_to_eat: Drink fresh, usually in small glasses.
how_to_order: Order 'uma poncha' in Madeira bars.

name: Madeira Wine
description: A fortified wine aged with heat, made on Madeira. 'Madeira' is an EU protected designation of origin.
how_to_eat: Drink as an aperitif or with dessert.
how_to_order: Taste it in Funchal wine lodges.

name: Bolo de Mel
description: A dark, dense spiced cake made with sugar-cane honey, considered Madeira's oldest dessert. It is traditionally made for Christmas.
how_to_eat: Break into pieces by hand rather than cutting.
how_to_order: Buy at Madeira bakeries and markets.

name: Espada com Banana
description: Fillets of black scabbardfish, caught in deep water off Madeira, fried and served with fried banana. It is the island's signature fish dish.
how_to_eat: Eat the fish together with the sweet fried banana.
how_to_order: Order 'espada com banana' in Funchal restaurants.
